metadata.summary: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and management of IgE-mediated egg allergy, primarily in children but also addressing adult patients. It covers epidemiology, risk factors, clinical presentation, diagnostic testing, dietary avoidance, egg reintroduction strategies, and the management of co-morbidities. Vaccination guidance for egg-allergic individuals and preventative measures, including early introduction of egg, are also included.

therapies_index.name: Egg avoidance diet
therapies_index.mechanism: Elimination of egg and egg-containing foods to prevent IgE-mediated allergic reactions.
approved_indications: Established egg allergy to avoid acute allergic reactions.
therapies_index.administration: Oral dietary restriction, with strict label reading and awareness of cross-contamination.
key_toxicities: Nutritional deficiencies (e.g., vitamin D, protein) if not properly substituted

therapies_index.name: Second-generation non-drowsy oral antihistamine
therapies_index.mechanism: H1 receptor antagonist, reduces histamine-mediated symptoms of mild allergic reactions.
approved_indications: Emergency treatment of mild allergic reactions following accidental egg ingestion.
therapies_index.administration: Oral, as needed per weight-appropriate dosing.

therapies_index.name: Adrenaline autoinjector
therapies_index.mechanism: Sympathomimetic agent; alpha- and beta-adrenergic agonist that reverses anaphylactic shock and airway obstruction.
approved_indications: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (severe allergic reactions) in egg-allergic patients with respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: Intramuscular injection via autoinjector device (e.g., EpiPen) into the anterolateral thigh.
monitoring: Annual specialist review to reassess need and provide training

therapies_index.name: Egg oral immunotherapy (OIT)
therapies_index.mechanism: Regular ingestion of gradually increasing amounts of egg protein to induce desensitization and potentially sustained unresponsiveness.
approved_indications: Persistent egg allergy in children over 5 years, under specialist supervision in highly specialized centres. Not recommended as standard therapy per EAACI.
therapies_index.administration: Oral daily dosing with controlled dose escalation; may be combined with baked egg protocols.
key_toxicities: High incidence of adverse reactions during build-up
Anaphylaxis (adrenaline required in 26% of children in one study)

therapies_index.name: Egg ladder (Home-based baked egg introduction)
therapies_index.mechanism: Gradual dietary reintroduction of egg in forms of increasing allergenicity (baked to raw) to assess tolerance and promote oral tolerance.
approved_indications: Children >12 months with mild-moderate egg allergy, mild reactions only, and no asthma, to achieve resolution at home.
therapies_index.administration: Oral, starting with a pea-sized amount of sponge cake (low egg content, well-baked), advancing per the BSACI egg ladder every few months if tolerated.
key_toxicities: Mild cutaneous reactions at very low starting doses; anaphylaxis not reported in home series.

therapies_index.name: Maternal egg exclusion diet
therapies_index.mechanism: Elimination of egg from the maternal diet to reduce secretion of egg protein into breast milk and thus reduce allergic symptoms in the breastfed infant.
approved_indications: Breastfed infants with persistent eczema where egg is a trigger, or suspected reactions to maternal egg ingestion.
therapies_index.administration: Oral maternal diet; strict avoidance for 4–6 weeks trial, then reintroduction to confirm effect.
key_toxicities: Maternal nutritional deficiency if prolonged and unsupervised

therapies_index.name: Measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine
therapies_index.mechanism: Active immunization using live attenuated viruses grown in chick embryo fibroblast cultures; vaccine does not contain significant egg protein.
approved_indications: All children with egg allergy should receive the MMR immunization as part of the routine vaccination schedule.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous injection in primary care; no special precautions for egg-allergic patients.
key_toxicities: Routine vaccine side effects unrelated to egg allergy; no increased risk of allergic reactions in egg-allergic children.

therapies_index.name: Influenza vaccine (inactivated and live attenuated)
therapies_index.mechanism: Vaccines derived from chicken embryos; most modern formulations contain very low ovalbumin levels (<0.12 mcg/mL) and are safe in egg allergy.
approved_indications: All egg-allergic children and adults can receive the influenza vaccine in primary care, except those who have had anaphylaxis to egg requiring intensive care admission.
therapies_index.administration: Intramuscular injection (inactivated) or intranasal spray (LAIV). The nasal LAIV is safe for egg-allergic children.
key_toxicities: Minimal egg-related allergic reactions due to very low ovalbumin content.
monitoring: Routine post-vaccination observation; those with history of severe anaphylaxis to egg should be referred to a specialist.

therapies_index.name: Yellow fever vaccine
therapies_index.mechanism: Live attenuated vaccine grown in hen's eggs; induces immunity against yellow fever virus.
approved_indications: Egg-allergic individuals travelling to yellow fever endemic areas; administration under specialist allergy guidance with risk assessment and possible desensitization.
therapies_index.administration: Subcutaneous injection given at designated Yellow Fever Vaccination Centres; may require skin testing and a split-dose protocol.
monitoring: Prior skin prick testing to egg and vaccine
Intradermal testing if initial skin test negative
Serological follow-up if skin test positive or desensitization used

therapies_index.name: Purified chick embryo cell (PCEC) rabies vaccine
therapies_index.mechanism: Inactivated rabies virus vaccine prepared in chick embryo cell culture; contains trace egg proteins.
approved_indications: For pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis against rabies in egg-allergic individuals; relative contraindication in those with egg anaphylaxis, but benefit outweighs risk for post-exposure.
key_toxicities: Allergic reactions including anaphylaxis in egg-sensitized individuals
monitoring: Observation after vaccination; risk assessment in those with severe egg allergy.

therapies_index.name: Psychological intervention
therapies_index.mechanism: Cognitive-behavioural therapy and other psychological techniques to reduce food allergy-related anxiety, phobias, and improve quality of life.
approved_indications: Egg-allergic patients with significant anxiety, post-traumatic stress following severe reactions, or impaired quality of life.
therapies_index.administration: Delivered via paediatric psychology services, CAMHS (children), or IAPT (adults).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: patients diagnosed with IgE-mediated egg allergy
decision_rules: clinical history and supportive testing (SPT ≥3 mm or positive specific IgE) confirm diagnosis
after acute reaction, initiate egg avoidance and provide emergency medication

recommended_regimens.name: Egg avoidance and emergency medication
recommended_regimens.summary: Strict dietary exclusion of egg, coupled with provision of an oral antihistamine; consider an adrenaline autoinjector if there is a history of anaphylaxis

supportive_care: referral to a dietitian for detailed avoidance guidance and nutritional assessment, especially when multiple food allergies or nutritional concerns exist
education on reading food labels and cross-contamination risks

treatment_pathways.patient_population: children with mild-moderate egg allergy (cutaneous reactions only), no asthma, who are candidates for home reintroduction
decision_rules: if reactions are mild and there is no asthma, home reintroduction can begin at 12 months of age or 6 months after the last reaction
start with small amounts of baked egg (Stage 1)
in case of mild symptoms, reduce to a lower stage or smaller amount; if symptoms persist, stop and seek medical advice
regular ingestion of baked egg may accelerate tolerance
after tolerating baked egg, progress to loosely cooked egg (Stage 2), then to raw egg (Stage 3)

recommended_regimens.name: Home-based egg reintroduction ladder
recommended_regimens.summary: Gradual, stepwise introduction of egg-containing foods following a three-stage ladder: Stage 1 – baked/well-cooked egg (e.g. cake, hard biscuits); Stage 2 – well-cooked egg dishes and loosely cooked egg (e.g. scrambled egg, omelette); Stage 3 – raw egg products (e.g. mayonnaise). Each stage is introduced in small amounts first.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: approximately one third of children outgrow well-cooked egg allergy by 3 years, and two-thirds by 6 years; tolerance to baked egg predicts eventual resolution
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: ongoing with regular ingestion; progress through stages as tolerated

response_assessment.timepoint: after each new food introduction and during routine follow-up
response_assessment.interpretation: tolerance to a stage is demonstrated by absence of immediate allergic reactions; progression to the next stage is appropriate after a period of consistent tolerance

supportive_care: dietitian referral if help with the reintroduction ladder is needed
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: families should be educated to recognize and manage possible allergic reactions; oral antihistamine should be available

treatment_pathways.patient_population: children with a history of severe egg reaction, severe eczema, or faltering growth
decision_rules: severe reactions (respiratory or cardiovascular involvement), severe eczema, or growth failure indicate a higher likelihood of persistent allergy
reintroduction must be guided by an allergy specialist

recommended_regimens.name: Specialist-guided egg reintroduction
recommended_regimens.summary: The same egg reintroduction ladder is followed, but under direct medical supervision in a specialist allergy clinic, with readiness to treat anaphylaxis
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: as tolerated, with possible progression over months to years

response_assessment.timepoint: during in-clinic challenges and follow-up visits
response_assessment.method: physician-observed food challenge with monitoring of symptoms and vital signs
response_assessment.interpretation: objective tolerance at each step determines progression

supportive_care: dietitian referral for advice on strict egg avoidance and nutritional support
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: excellent asthma control is a priority before any attempt at reintroduction

treatment_pathways.patient_population: children with persistent egg allergy, typically over 5 years of age, who have not outgrown allergy despite baked egg introduction
decision_rules: egg OIT is not recommended as a routine treatment for long-term tolerance
it may be considered only in highly specialized allergy centres for carefully selected patients with persistent disease

alternative_regimens.name: Egg oral immunotherapy (OIT)
alternative_regimens.summary: Gradual ingestion of increasing amounts of egg protein under medical supervision, aiming to induce desensitization. Daily dosing is more effective than weekly. Low pretreatment egg white and ovomucoid IgE predict sustained unresponsiveness.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: only in highly specialized allergy centres; not for routine clinical use

not_recommended.name: Routine use of egg OIT
not_recommended.reason: high incidence of adverse events (adrenaline required in 26% of children in one study), absence of standardized protocols, and low-quality evidence for long-term tolerance

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: EAACI does not currently recommend egg OIT as a treatment to achieve long-term tolerance

treatment_pathways.patient_population: egg-allergic patients of any age requiring routine vaccination with MMR, influenza, or yellow fever
decision_rules: MMR vaccine: administer in primary care without special precautions (Grade B)

influenza vaccine (nasal live attenuated or intramuscular): can be given in primary care unless there has been anaphylaxis to egg requiring intensive care admission; in that case, refer to an allergy specialist (Grade B)
yellow fever vaccine: contains egg protein; always refer to an allergy specialist with access to a designated yellow fever vaccination centre for assessment and administration (Grade B)

recommended_regimens.name: Vaccination protocol for egg allergy
recommended_regimens.summary: MMR given routinely; influenza given in primary care with observation, except after severe anaphylaxis; yellow fever given only under specialist supervision in a designated centre

treatment_pathways.patient_population: adults with egg allergy, including those with persistent childhood-onset allergy and new adult-onset disease
decision_rules: egg avoidance and emergency medication training are the mainstay
periodic measurement of specific IgE to monitor allergy status
component testing (particularly Gal d 1/ovomucoid) can help select patients for oral food challenges; a negative Gal d 1 test suggests baked egg might be tolerated
oral food challenges should be considered to establish the likelihood of tolerance, as fatal anaphylaxis has been reported

recommended_regimens.name: Egg avoidance and emergency medication (adult)
recommended_regimens.summary: Strict avoidance of egg, availability of antihistamine and adrenaline autoinjector, and periodic reassessment with specialist advice
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: lifelong, though tolerance may develop; periodic reevaluation is advised

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: occupational egg allergy (e.g. in bakers) and bird-egg syndrome should be identified and managed accordingly

treatment_pathways.patient_population: infants with eczema, who are at high risk of developing egg allergy
decision_rules: early introduction of well-cooked or baked egg into the diet reduces the incidence of egg allergy
introduce egg around 6 months of age (but not before 4 months) and ensure regular ongoing consumption

recommended_regimens.name: Early egg introduction for prevention
recommended_regimens.summary: Feed infants with eczema well-cooked or baked egg starting around 6 months of age to reduce the risk of developing egg allergy
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: regular consumption as part of the diet

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: do not introduce egg if the infant already has a confirmed egg allergy; this pathway is for primary prevention only

conditions.name: Egg allergy
conditions.description: An adverse immunologic reaction to egg proteins, primarily ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and ovomucoid (Gal d 1), mediated by specific IgE antibodies. The reaction is typically immediate type-1 hypersensitivity with rapid symptom onset; late-phase and delayed hypersensitivity reactions can also occur, particularly in the context of eczema.
conditions.epidemiology: Prevalence is approximately 2% in children and 0.1% in adults in the United Kingdom. Onset most commonly occurs in infancy, often after the first apparent ingestion; new-onset egg allergy in adults is rare.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Typical presentation is in infancy, with rapid onset (within minutes) of cutaneous symptoms (erythema, urticaria, angioedema) and/or vomiting following egg ingestion. Severe reactions are less common and may involve respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, breathing difficulty) or cardiovascular symptoms (pallor, floppiness). Reaction severity is influenced by the amount of egg ingested and the degree of cooking; raw egg white is the most allergenic form. Delayed worsening of eczema may also occur.

subtypes.name: Childhood-onset egg allergy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually presents in infancy, often with mild to moderate symptoms; high rate of spontaneous resolution by adolescence; commonly associated with other atopic conditions such as eczema and asthma.

subtypes.name: Adult-onset egg allergy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Rare; may occur as new onset in adulthood after years of tolerance, or as persistence of childhood allergy; tends to be more severe and persistent; can be associated with bird-egg syndrome or occupational sensitization.

subtypes.name: Occupational egg allergy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Results from inhalation of egg protein aerosols in occupational settings (e.g., baking industry); may develop respiratory symptoms and subsequently react upon ingestion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To establish a diagnosis of egg allergy based on typical symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: All patients with suspected egg allergy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Rapid onset (minutes) of erythema, urticaria, angioedema, and/or vomiting after egg ingestion is highly suggestive. Mild reactions in a clear history are sufficient for diagnosis without further testing.

diagnostic_workup.test: Skin prick test (SPT) with standardized whole egg reagent
diagnostic_workup.purpose: To confirm IgE sensitization to egg.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Moderate‑severe reactions, or when the clinical history is unclear.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A weal size of ≥3 mm in combination with a supportive clinical history is diagnostic in most cases. Higher cut‑offs (e.g., ≥5 mm in children under 2 years) increase specificity. SPT weal size does not predict clinical severity. SPT should not be used for screening in the absence of suspected reaction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To detect circulating egg‑specific IgE antibodies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When SPT is unavailable, or in moderate‑severe cases to support diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No single diagnostic cut‑off value is applicable across all ages; low levels can be found in egg‑tolerant children. Therefore, results must be correlated with clinical history. Egg‑specific IgE should not be measured in asymptomatic individuals as it may lead to unnecessary dietary restriction.

diagnostic_workup.test: Component‑resolved diagnostics (specific IgE to Gal d 1, Gal d 2, Gal d 3, Gal d 5)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: To identify sensitization to individual egg allergens, which aids in predicting persistence and tolerance to baked egg.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessing likelihood of resolution, especially in older children or adults; may guide decisions on oral food challenge.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Sensitization to multiple components, particularly Gal d 1 (ovomucoid), suggests persistent allergy. Negative Gal d 1 IgE is associated with a higher chance of tolerating baked egg. Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) IgE is common but less predictive of severity. Gal d 5 indicates egg yolk allergy and possible bird‑egg syndrome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To definitively confirm or refute the diagnosis, or to prove tolerance has developed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinical history and test results are discordant, or to assess resolution of allergy. Hospital‑based challenges are reserved for high‑risk patients (Box 4).
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A controlled graded ingestion of egg (baked, lightly cooked, or raw) under medical supervision; positive if objective allergic symptoms occur. Baked egg challenges are used to determine if heat‑processed egg is tolerated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To detect sensitization to raw egg proteins.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not routinely recommended; may be considered in research settings.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A weal of ≥13 mm has been reported as diagnostic. Does not predict baked egg tolerance and carries a risk of systemic reaction; not standardized.

diagnostic_workup.test: Skin prick test with baked egg slurry
diagnostic_workup.purpose: To predict the outcome of a baked egg challenge.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Research setting; not routinely used in clinical practice.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: High negative predictive value reported in one study.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To assess risk of peanut allergy and guide early peanut introduction advice.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Egg allergy in infancy is associated with increased risk of peanut allergy; early peanut introduction may prevent its development.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Indicates sensitization to egg white proteins; supports clinical diagnosis when history is positive but not diagnostic in isolation.
Major heat‑labile egg white allergen; commonly detected in egg‑allergic individuals.
Heat‑stable and immunodominant allergen; sensitization is associated with persistent egg allergy, greater severity, and reduced likelihood of baked egg tolerance.
Egg white allergen; may contribute to sensitization profile.
Egg yolk allergen; marker for bird‑egg syndrome; indicates cross‑reactivity with bird feather allergens.

pathology_markers.marker: Skin prick test weal diameter (to egg white)
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Supports diagnosis of egg allergy when combined with history; larger weals increase specificity but do not correlate with severity.

prognostic_tools.name: Prognostic indicators for resolution of egg allergy
components: Age at tolerance to baked egg
Sensitization to multiple egg allergen components (especially ovomucoid/Gal d 1)

risk_groups.criteria: Mild or cutaneous‑only initial reactions, no asthma, low egg‑specific IgE, early tolerance of baked egg, absence of ovomucoid or multi‑component sensitization, and no other food allergies or severe eczema.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: High likelihood of outgrowing allergy; median age of resolution for well‑cooked egg is 67 months and for uncooked egg 127 months; approximately 68% resolve by 16 years.

risk_groups.criteria: History of respiratory or cardiovascular severe reactions, presence of asthma or severe eczema, high egg‑specific IgE, sensitization to multiple components (especially ovomucoid), and multiple food allergies.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: More likely to have persistent allergy into adolescence or adulthood; delayed achievement of tolerance to well‑cooked egg and uncooked egg.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: These factors guide the timing and setting of egg reintroduction (home vs hospital) and the need for specialist allergy follow‑up. Children with favorable features may attempt home‑based baked egg introduction from 12 months.

follow_up.schedule: All infants and young children with egg allergy should be periodically assessed for suitability of reintroduction. Adults and older children with persistent egg allergy should be reviewed at intervals to update emergency medication training, repeat specific IgE testing, and consider component testing and oral food challenges to determine if resolution has occurred. Exact frequency is not specified but typically annual or as guided by clinical progress.
recommended_tests: Interval clinical history (new reactions, dietary adherence, growth)
Egg‑specific IgE (and possibly component IgE) to monitor sensitization trends
Consideration of oral food challenge to baked egg or cooked egg when prognostic factors are favorable
long_term_effects: Risk of accidental anaphylaxis, including fatalities
Dietary restrictions impacting quality of life and social participation
Psychosocial burden: anxiety, bullying, family stress
Potential for nutritional deficiencies if multiple food allergies
In persistent cases, lifelong egg avoidance may be required
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Many children outgrow egg allergy; early introduction of baked egg may accelerate tolerance. Adults with persistent allergy should receive ongoing support and education. All patients need an up‑to‑date emergency management plan and ready access to antihistamines and adrenaline auto‑injectors.

conditions.name: Bird‑egg syndrome
synonyms: Egg yolk allergy with bird feather sensitization
conditions.description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
conditions.epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.

diagnostic_workup.test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
diagnostic_workup.purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
diagnostic_workup.purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.

follow_up.schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
long_term_effects: Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
follow_up.survivorship_notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

toxicities.event: Acute IgE-mediated allergic reaction to egg
toxicities.incidence: Cutaneous symptoms in 80-90%, gastrointestinal in 10-44% within minutes to 2 hours. Anaphylaxis prior to allergy service referral in 7%. Fatal anaphylaxis reported in one adult in the UK since 1992.
recognition: Rapid onset (within minutes) of erythema, urticaria, angioedema
Severe: respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, stridor, breathing difficulty), cardiovascular (pallor, floppiness)

management.actions: Administer non-drowsy second-generation antihistamine; observe at home.
Administer intramuscular adrenaline; seek emergency medical attention; provide anaphylaxis plan and regular review by allergy specialist.

prevention: Strict dietary avoidance of egg and egg-containing products
Read food labels carefully, as egg is declared as a priority allergen in the EU
Avoid loose foods and buffets in severe cases
Referral to a dietician for avoidance advice

toxicities.event: Allergic reaction during home-based egg reintroduction
toxicities.incidence: In a cohort of 211 children undergoing home baked egg introduction, no anaphylaxis was reported. Risk of anaphylaxis is considered minimal when using a gradual, low-dose approach starting at approximately 20 mg egg protein.
recognition: Symptoms usually mild, e.g., cutaneous reactions

management.actions: Stop the reintroduction, revert to the previously tolerated step in the ladder, and consider re-attempting gradual introduction after 3-6 months.

prevention: Gradual, staged, low-dose approach according to the egg ladder
Do not attempt within 6 months of a significant allergic reaction to egg

Exclude patients with history of severe reactions, poorly controlled asthma, severe eczema (>40% body surface), severe multisystem allergic disease, or recent trace reactions from home introduction; these require hospital-based challenge

toxicities.event: Adverse reaction during hospital-based egg challenge
toxicities.incidence: Adrenaline required in 2% of 236 children in one study; no adrenaline needed in 181 challenges. In another study of 678 challenges, two children meeting home introduction criteria developed airway symptoms, but these challenges used higher starting doses (200 mg egg protein) and rapid escalation compared to gradual home introduction (starting 20 mg).
recognition: Rapid onset of allergic symptoms following ingestion, monitored in hospital setting

management.actions: Challenge conducted under medical supervision with immediate access to emergency medications including adrenaline; appropriate treatment according to reaction severity.

prevention: Select patients for hospital challenge according to criteria: severe previous reactions, asthma, severe eczema, multisystem disease, high anxiety, persistent egg allergy, etc.
Use low starting doses and gradual escalation

toxicities.event: Adverse reactions to egg oral immunotherapy
toxicities.incidence: High incidence of adverse events; in one study, adrenaline required in 26% of children. Early discontinuation associated with asthma, higher specific IgE, and lower reaction threshold. Ovomucoid IgE >8.85 kU/L indicates 95% probability of early discontinuation or persistent reactions.
recognition: Allergic symptoms during dose escalation, including anaphylaxis

management.actions: Discontinue immunotherapy and treat according to anaphylaxis protocol; OIT should only be performed in highly specialized allergy centres.

prevention: EAACI does not currently recommend egg OIT for long-term tolerance in children with persistent egg allergy
Should only be undertaken in highly specialized centres
Consider predictors: high ovomucoid IgE, asthma, lower reaction threshold

toxicities.event: Eosinophilic esophagitis as complication of egg oral immunotherapy
toxicities.incidence: Has been reported as a complication; usually reversible after early diagnosis and stopping immunotherapy.
recognition: Symptoms of esophageal dysfunction (not specified in detail, likely dysphagia, food impaction)

management.actions: Stop immunotherapy; condition is usually reversible.

prevention: Early diagnosis by monitoring for symptoms

toxicities.event: Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) to egg
toxicities.incidence: Egg is a common trigger; 30% of infants with milk or soy FPIES also react to egg. Resolution typically by around 42 months, with tolerance to baked egg occurring earlier (around 30 months) than raw egg (43 months).
recognition: Recurrent vomiting, fluid loss, dehydration, shock occurring within 4 hours of ingestion

management.actions: Rapid intravenous fluid resuscitation may be needed; management in a centre experienced in food challenges with prolonged observation.
Confirm resolution by supervised food challenge in an appropriate facility.

prevention: Avoidance of egg protein; cautious introduction of baked egg under supervision may be tolerated before raw egg.

toxicities.event: Hypersensitivity reaction to propofol in egg-allergic patients
toxicities.incidence: One case reported of a child with egg anaphylaxis developing urticaria and erythema on two occasions after propofol. Generally considered safe in egg-allergic patients, both children and adults.

management.actions: Treat with antihistamines; no specific contraindication, propofol may still be used.

prevention: Propofol can be used safely in egg-allergic patients; no specific preventive measures required.

toxicities.event: Allergic reaction to influenza vaccine in egg-allergic patients
toxicities.incidence: Reports of egg-related allergic reactions are now largely historical. Ovalbumin content in most current vaccines is <0.12 mcg/ml (<0.06 mcg per 0.5 ml dose). Safe even in those with previous egg anaphylaxis. No safety data on children with anaphylaxis requiring ICU admission.

management.actions: Observe for 30 minutes post-vaccination; treat with antihistamines if needed.

management.severity: history of anaphylaxis to egg requiring ICU
management.actions: Refer to specialist for supervised immunization or consider egg-free influenza vaccine if available and age-appropriate.

prevention: Use vaccines with low ovalbumin content
Routine administration in primary care for most egg-allergic patients
For those with life-threatening anaphylaxis to egg requiring ICU, specialist assessment recommended

toxicities.event: Allergic reaction to yellow fever vaccine in egg-allergic patients
toxicities.incidence: Rate of anaphylaxis: 1 in 238,000 doses when given alone, 1 in 131,000 when co-administered.
recognition: Anaphylactic symptoms; thought to be related to residual egg protein, though other allergens possible.

management.actions: Refer to allergy specialist at least 2 months before travel; perform skin prick test to egg and undiluted vaccine; if negative, intradermal test at 1:10 or 1:100 dilution. Negative IDT predicts tolerance; proceed with vaccine. Positive testing: consider certificate of exemption if travel not essential, or if seroconversion not confirmed, or perform 7-step desensitization regime.
Treat per anaphylaxis protocol in vaccination centre.

prevention: Specialist allergy centre assessment with skin testing and possible graded dosing or desensitization; collaboration with Yellow Fever Vaccination Centre

toxicities.event: Allergic reaction to purified chick embryo cell (PCEC) rabies vaccine
toxicities.incidence: Reports of allergic reactions and anaphylaxis, some possibly related to egg allergy.

management.severity: post-exposure prophylaxis in egg-allergic patient with anaphylaxis history
management.actions: Use human diploid cell vaccine (egg-free) if available; if PCEC is only option, administer under close monitoring due to high fatality of rabies, risk of vaccine reaction is outweighed.

prevention: Avoid PCEC in those with previous egg anaphylaxis if alternative egg-free vaccine available; post-exposure prophylaxis necessity overrides relative contraindication

prophylaxis.recommendation: Strict avoidance of egg and egg-containing foods; read labels; avoid loose foods and buffets if severe allergy.

Prescribe non-drowsy antihistamine for all; adrenaline autoinjector for those with history of severe reactions, asthma on preventer, or persistent allergy. Provide anaphylaxis action plan and annual review.
prophylaxis.target_population: all patients: antihistamine; autoinjector: severe reactors

prophylaxis.recommendation: Refer to dietician for multiple food allergies, nutritional concerns, severe egg allergy requiring strict avoidance, or assistance with reintroduction ladder.
Most mothers should continue unrestricted diet; consider maternal egg exclusion for 4-6 weeks if persistent eczema triggered by egg or suspected infant reaction, then reintroduce.
Introduce well-cooked egg early (from 4-6 months) in infants with eczema, starting with small amounts, to reduce risk of egg allergy.
Introduce peanut early in egg-allergic infants under 11 months to reduce risk of peanut allergy.
Most egg-allergic children and adults can receive influenza vaccine in primary care; refer those with anaphylaxis to egg requiring ICU to specialist.
Refer to allergy specialist for assessment before yellow fever vaccination; skin testing, possible desensitization if necessary.
All children with egg allergy should receive MMR vaccine in primary care without special precautions.
For post-exposure prophylaxis, use egg-free human diploid cell vaccine if available; if PCEC only option, administer with caution as benefit outweighs risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: egg-allergic patients with history of anaphylaxis

special_populations.considerations: Mothers may consider trying egg exclusion from their diet if the infant has persistent eczema and egg is a trigger, or if the infant is suspected of reacting to maternal egg ingestion. Most infants should continue breastfeeding with the mother on an unrestricted diet.

Infants with eczema are at higher risk of developing egg allergy. Early introduction of well‑cooked or baked egg into the diet from 4–6 months of age reduces the incidence of egg allergy (Grade A recommendation). Infants with moderate‑severe eczema or existing food allergy are at highest risk of reacting on initial egg introduction, so the first ingestions should be in tiny (pea‑sized) amounts.

special_populations.population: Children with severe eczema or faltering growth
special_populations.considerations: These children are more likely to have persistent egg allergy. Avoidance and reintroduction should be guided by a specialist allergy service.

special_populations.population: Children with a history of severe reaction to egg
special_populations.considerations: Home reintroduction should not be attempted if previous reactions involved severe gastrointestinal, respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms. Hospital‑based egg challenge should be considered. This includes patients with egg allergy and severe/poorly controlled asthma.

special_populations.population: Patients with asthma and egg allergy
special_populations.considerations: Patients with severe or poorly controlled asthma should undergo hospital‑based egg challenge. Those with well‑controlled mild asthma may attempt home introduction if they have only had mild cutaneous reactions.
Egg allergy in adults is rare, usually more severe, and tends to persist.

Yellow fever vaccines contain detectable amounts of egg protein. Egg‑allergic patients requiring this vaccine should be referred to an allergy specialist with access to a designated yellow fever vaccination centre for assessment and immunization.

special_populations.population: Egg‑allergic patients on biologics or immunosuppressants
special_populations.considerations: These patients should be referred to an allergy clinic. They are also a relative indication for hospital‑based egg challenge.

special_populations.population: Children with high anxiety or inability to adhere to a home introduction protocol
special_populations.considerations: Home introduction may not be appropriate; specialist referral or hospital‑based challenge may be needed. Children with communication disorders may benefit from home introduction to avoid hospital‑related anxiety.

special_populations.population: Older children with persistent egg allergy
special_populations.considerations: A more cautious approach to home reintroduction should be taken, and hospital challenge may be considered.

recommendations.statement: Allergic sensitization to egg without a history of reacting should not prevent the introduction of egg into the diet, as this carries a risk of unnecessary dietary exclusion.
In moderate-severe cases or where there is diagnostic uncertainty, measuring egg-specific IgE or performing skin prick testing is useful.
An egg skin prick test weal of 3 mm or more, combined with a compatible clinical history, is considered adequate to confirm a diagnosis of egg allergy in most cases.
Clinical severity cannot be judged on the basis of skin prick test weal size or serum-specific IgE alone.
In the absence of a suspected reaction, patients should not be routinely tested for egg allergy.
A food challenge may be necessary to confirm or refute conflicting history and test results but is rarely required in practice to confirm the diagnosis of egg allergy.
Following an acute allergic reaction to egg, egg avoidance advice is the cornerstone of management.
Most infants with egg allergy should continue to breastfeed, with their mother on an unrestricted diet.

Mothers breastfeeding egg-allergic infants may wish to try egg exclusion if their infants have persistent eczema and egg is a trigger, or if the infant is suspected of reacting to maternal egg ingestion.
Referral to a dietician is required if there are multiple food allergies, nutritional concerns, or help is needed following the reintroduction ladder.
Referral to a dietician is needed for children with severe egg allergy for advice about strict egg avoidance.
Mild egg allergy usually resolves; attempts to introduce baked egg as an ingredient (e.g. in cake) may be made from the age of 12 months, or 6 months from the last reaction.
Regular ingestion of baked egg may promote tolerance and should be encouraged.
Once loosely cooked egg is tolerated, egg allergy is outgrown and egg should be eaten as part of the normal diet.

Resolution occurs gradually over time; assessment for reintroduction of baked egg in all infants and young children presenting with egg allergy is advised, as prolonged total exclusion may lead to more persistent allergy and increases dietary and social exclusion.
Children with mild-moderate symptoms can reintroduce egg at home, starting with baked egg in small amounts.

Children with a history of a severe egg reaction or severe eczema and faltering growth are more likely to have persistent disease; avoidance and reintroduction should be guided by a specialist allergy service.
Early introduction of well-cooked or baked egg into the diet of infants with eczema reduces the incidence of egg allergy and is recommended.
Egg allergy in infancy is associated with an increased risk of developing peanut allergy; early introduction of peanut into the diet is recommended to prevent this.
All children with egg allergy should receive the MMR immunization in primary care.

Children with egg allergy can receive the nasal live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV), and most children and adults can receive the intramuscular influenza vaccine in primary care, unless they have had anaphylaxis to egg requiring admission to intensive care.
If yellow fever vaccine is required, the egg-allergic patient should be referred to an allergy specialist with access to a designated yellow fever vaccination centre for assessment and immunization.

Referral to an allergy clinic is recommended for patients with egg allergy in the following circumstances: history of moderate to severe reaction, diagnostic uncertainty, association with other IgE-mediated food allergies, severe eczema on an egg-containing diet, allergy to baked egg persisting beyond 6–7 years, adult-onset egg allergy, requirement for yellow fever immunisation, inability to reintroduce egg due to high anxiety, or use of biologics/immunosuppressants.

recommendations.statement: For the diagnosis of egg allergy: most children should receive a clinical diagnosis without food challenge; a negative skin prick test can exclude egg allergy if the history is unclear; skin prick test weal size or specific IgE level do not predict severity; the severity of a reaction depends on the amount of allergen ingested, the matrix, how well it is cooked, and concomitant asthma, exercise or illness.
recommendations.source_heading: BOX 2 Making a diagnosis of egg allergy

recommendations.statement: Hospital-based egg challenge should be considered after an interval of >1 year from the last reaction in patients with: severe symptoms affecting breathing, circulation, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; severe/poorly controlled asthma; severe multisystem allergic disease. Relative indications include: mild-moderate reactions to trace exposure, stable asthma on regular preventer, multiple complex food allergies, inability to adhere to a protocol, high anxiety, immunosuppressant or biologic use, and older patients with persistent egg allergy.
recommendations.source_heading: BOX 4 Hospital based egg challenge should be considered...

recommendations.statement: Skin testing with raw egg is not routinely recommended outside research settings because it lacks standardization and carries a risk of severe reactions.
Measurement of peanut-specific IgE should be included in infants with moderate/severe egg allergy to guide peanut allergy prevention advice.
Egg component testing is rarely needed for the routine diagnosis and management of egg allergy in children but can be a useful adjunct for the assessment of egg allergy resolution in adults.
Those avoiding hen's egg should also avoid eggs from other avian species, such as duck, goose and quail, due to common cross-reactivity.
recommendations.source_heading: 8.4 Cross-reactivity between eggs from hens and other bird species

recommendations.statement: All families with egg-allergic children should have an appropriate oral antihistamine available, preferably a second-generation, non-drowsy antihistamine, to treat allergic reactions due to accidental ingestion.
recommendations.source_heading: 8.6 Provision of emergency medication and treatment plans

recommendations.statement: Children with egg allergy and asthma requiring regular preventative treatment with inhaled corticosteroids should be considered for an adrenaline autoinjector.
recommendations.source_heading: 8.6 Provision of emergency medication and treatment plans

recommendations.statement: Families should receive training in how to use their emergency medication, including demonstration with a trainer device and provision of a management plan.
recommendations.source_heading: 8.6 Provision of emergency medication and treatment plans

recommendations.statement: Adults and young people with persisting egg allergy should be re-assessed, especially prior to a move away from home, and provided with updated dietary management advice and review of the need for an adrenaline autoinjector.
recommendations.source_heading: 8.6 Provision of emergency medication and treatment plans

recommendations.statement: If a reaction occurs during home reintroduction, the previously tolerated diet should be followed, and further reintroduction considered after 3–6 months.
Egg introduction or challenge should not be deferred for concern of increasing sensitization.
Children with severe egg allergy should be followed up periodically to assess the likelihood of resolution and to refresh avoidance advice and emergency medication training.
Reintroduction can be attempted if there has been no significant recent clinical reaction, accompanied by a reduction in SPT wheal size or serum-specific IgE over time.
Children with severe egg allergy should have a supervised challenge in hospital, not at home.
Egg oral immunotherapy should only be undertaken in highly specialized allergy centres.

Older children or adults with pre-existing egg allergy should be assessed for the likely resolution of egg allergy; component testing can be useful in determining whether a baked egg challenge might be tolerated.
Excellent asthma control should be a priority in children with egg allergy, as the presence of asthma may increase the potential severity of accidental egg reactions.
Propofol is safe to use in children with egg allergy.
recommendations.source_heading: 11.4 Use of Propofol in egg-allergic patients

recommendations.statement: Resolution of food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) to egg should be confirmed by food challenge in a centre with experience in food challenges, facilities for rapid intravenous fluid resuscitation, and prolonged observation.
Egg-allergic patients requiring yellow fever vaccine should be assessed in a specialist allergy centre, ideally at least 2 months prior to travel.

If yellow fever immunization is not given after assessment, consider a certificate of exemption after serological confirmation if intradermal testing was performed; if no seroconversion, a desensitization regime may be considered.

Infants with moderate-severe or early-onset eczema or existing food allergy should have the first couple of ingestions of baked egg in tiny (pea-sized) amounts due to higher risk of reacting on initial introduction.

artifacts.summary: Compilation of the main evidence-based recommendations from the guideline, each accompanied by its SIGN-derived grade of recommendation (A–D). It covers epidemiology, diagnosis, management, resolution, vaccination, and prevention.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Serves as a quick reference for clinicians to understand the strength of recommendations on critical aspects of egg allergy care.

artifacts.title: Figure 3: Persistence of Egg Allergy to Cooked vs. Uncooked Egg
artifacts.description: Kaplan–Meier survival curves displaying the proportion of children remaining allergic to well-cooked egg and to uncooked egg over time. The log-rank test shows a significant difference between the two curves (p < 0.0001). Median age of tolerance acquisition is 67 months (5.6 years) for well-cooked egg and 127 months (10.3 years) for uncooked egg.
artifacts.summary: Graphical comparison of allergy persistence demonstrating that tolerance to extensively heated egg develops earlier and more quickly than tolerance to raw egg.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Reinforces the prognostic importance of baked egg tolerance and underpins the rationale for early baked egg introduction to accelerate allergy resolution.
